summary: Zinc gluconate is an oral zinc salt used as a dietary supplement to prevent or treat zinc deficiency and is widely marketed for immune support and to shorten the duration of the common cold. Zinc is an essential trace element required by numerous metalloenzymes for protein and DNA synthesis, immune function, wound healing, and sense of taste and smell. It is generally safe within recommended dietary allowances; excessive or prolonged high intake can cause gastrointestinal upset and copper deficiency (with anemia and neuropathy). Intranasal zinc gluconate products have been associated with loss of smell and should be avoided.

moa: Zinc gluconate dissociates to release elemental zinc, an essential trace mineral that serves as a catalytic, structural, or regulatory cofactor for more than 200 enzymes (metalloenzymes), including carbonic anhydrase, alkaline phosphatase, RNA and DNA polymerases, and superoxide dismutase. Through these enzymes zinc is essential for nucleic acid and protein synthesis, cell division and growth, normal immune function, wound healing, and the senses of taste and smell, and it stabilizes biological membranes. Supplementation restores adequate zinc-dependent enzyme activity in deficiency states; in the common cold, zinc ions are thought to interfere with rhinovirus replication and modulate inflammatory mediators.

Serum zinc in suspected deficiency or toxicity

preg: Zinc is an essential nutrient and is considered safe during pregnancy within the recommended dietary allowance (approximately 11-12 mg elemental zinc per day). High supratherapeutic doses should be avoided unless medically indicated for documented deficiency.
lact: Zinc is present in breast milk and is required for the breastfed infant. Supplementation within the recommended dietary allowance (about 12-13 mg elemental zinc per day for lactating women) is considered safe; avoid excessive doses.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is needed at supplemental doses. Use caution with high-dose or prolonged zinc supplementation in patients with renal failure or on dialysis, as accumulation and altered trace-element balance can occur; monitor as clinically indicated.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is required at usual supplemental doses. Zinc is sometimes used therapeutically (as zinc acetate) in Wilson disease to block copper absorption; otherwise no special hepatic precautions apply at nutritional doses.

major: Penicillamine and other copper chelators - zinc further depletes copper; monitor closely
moderate: Tetracycline and fluoroquinolone antibiotics - zinc reduces their absorption; separate dosing by at least 2-4 hours
Iron and calcium supplements - compete with zinc for absorption; separate dosing
High-dose zinc - induces metallothionein and causes copper deficiency over time
minor: Thiazide diuretics - may increase urinary zinc loss with long-term use
interactions.food: Food (especially phytates in whole grains/legumes) and dairy can reduce zinc absorption; take separately when feasible.
interactions.alcohol: Chronic alcohol intake decreases zinc absorption and increases urinary loss; limit alcohol.
interactions.diagnostics: Excess zinc can lower serum copper and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol; may cause copper-deficiency anemia/neutropenia on blood counts.

pearls: Zinc gluconate is about 14.3% elemental zinc - dose by elemental content
Long-term high-dose zinc (>40 mg/day) causes copper deficiency, anemia, neutropenia, and neuropathy - check copper
Separate from tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, iron, and calcium to avoid absorption interactions
Avoid intranasal zinc gluconate - linked to permanent anosmia
Cold-symptom benefit is modest and inconsistent; start within 24 hours if used

missed: If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip it. Do not take a double dose. For a daily supplement, simply resume your usual schedule.
overdose: Acute ingestion of large amounts can cause nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, diarrhea, and gastrointestinal corrosion; very large doses may cause dehydration and electrolyte disturbance. Chronic excess causes copper deficiency with anemia, neutropenia, and neuropathy. Management is supportive: stop zinc, give symptomatic GI care and fluids; chelation (e.g., with a copper-replenishing approach) is rarely needed. Milk or chelating agents may reduce absorption acutely.
